description: Hi, I’m Abhishek, a student at IIT Mandi working on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Our team is looking for members with skills in Python, data analysis, frontend development, or astronomy. Beginners who are curious and committed are welcome!
summary:
ParallaX is a free web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx images of any patch of sky into a short "blink" video, so anyone can spot stars and brown dwarfs that move and objects that change brightness. It is the blink comparator that found Pluto in 1930, rebuilt for a telescope that sees the whole sky in 102 infrared colours.

It answers the challenge directly. Type a star name or coordinates, and ParallaX finds every SPHEREx frame of that patch in the archive, groups the frames into visits, stacks each visit in six infrared bands, and blinks them. It works out of the box on all five challenge targets.

The key idea: each SPHEREx exposure sees a different wavelength, so blinking raw exposures shows a spectrum, not motion. ParallaX blinks one stack per visit per band instead, so only real motion and real variability remain.

It matters because volunteers blinking WISE images found more than 3,000 brown dwarfs. WISE has stopped observing, and SPHEREx, which re-images the whole sky every six months, had no public blink tool.
details:
What it does.

  • Type a star name or coordinates. ParallaX finds every SPHEREx frame of that patch, groups the frames into visits, stacks each visit in six infrared bands on one shared grid and brightness scale with north up, and plays the visits as a blink. Moving stars hop; varying objects pulse.
  • One-click missions cover the five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, ε Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.
  • On top of the blink:
  • - a measured proper-motion vector
  • - spectra built from the native frames
  • - light curves with a period search
  • - a wavelength-matched difference image
  • - a spectral flipbook
  • - a 25-year blink against 2MASS and WISE
  • - a mover finder
  • - Gaia, SIMBAD and AllWISE overlays
  • - Solar System tracking via JPL Horizons
  • It also spots when typed coordinates are an old position of a fast-moving star. The challenge's own WISE 0855 coordinate is a 2010 position, and ParallaX says so and shows where the object is now.

How it works.

  • A Python backend reads SPHEREx Quick Release frames from NASA/IPAC IRSA and the public AWS S3 bucket, and applies the official calibration files (wavelength maps, PSFs, pixel solid angles), locked by checksum.
  • Measurements always use the native frames, never the display stacks.
  • Light curves use a joint fit across wavelength channels, so slow variables like R Draconis keep their true amplitude.
  • Astrometry is registered to Gaia stars at each frame's epoch.

Benefits.

  • No login, and it works on a phone.
  • A PNG fallback covers devices without WebGL, and everything works from the keyboard.
  • The interface is in English, Hindi and Spanish.
  • Every view is a shareable or embeddable link.
  • Each view links out to WiseView, Legacy Survey, ESASky and SIMBAD.
  • Candidate reports copy as plain text for citizen-science forums.

Intended impact. Give the volunteers who found brown dwarfs in WISE a tool for SPHEREx from its first public releases onward. Each new data release is one configuration entry.

How it's creative.

  • It solves the problem specific to SPHEREx: each raw exposure sees a different colour, so a naive blink shows spectra, not motion. ParallaX stacks per visit per band instead.
  • It also spots catalogue positions that are out of date because the object has moved.

What we considered.

  • Scientific honesty: no fallback that could create false signals, and stated limits.
  • Reproducibility: the same link gives the same pixels.
  • Accessibility, low-bandwidth use, archive outages (a frozen offline copy), and data licensing.

Tools.

  • Python: FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, photutils.
  • TypeScript: React, WebGL2.
  • Aladin Lite, Docker, GitHub Actions.
